column1: 1:1|The record of the origins of Jesus the Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham.|Keeps genesis/origins broader than a mere name list and preserves the two defining ancestral titles.
1:2|Abraham fathered Isaac; Isaac fathered Jacob; Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.|Retains the repeated begetting pattern and Judah’s brothers.
1:3|Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar; Perez fathered Hezron; Hezron fathered Ram.|Preserves both twins, mother, and exact sequence.
1:4|Ram fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon.|Keeps the three linked generations in the same cadence.
1:5|Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab; Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth; Obed fathered Jesse.|Retains both named women and every relationship.
1:6|Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by Uriah’s wife.|Keeps king attached to David and the deliberate identification through Uriah rather than supplying Bathsheba.
1:7|Solomon fathered Rehoboam; Rehoboam fathered Abijah; Abijah fathered Asaph.|Follows pinned Asaph rather than harmonizing to Asa.
1:8|Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat; Jehoshaphat fathered Joram; Joram fathered Uzziah.|Retains the source’s compressed genealogy without inserting omitted kings.
1:9|Uzziah fathered Jotham; Jotham fathered Ahaz; Ahaz fathered Hezekiah.|Preserves the three royal links and established names.
1:10|Hezekiah fathered Manasseh; Manasseh fathered Amos; Amos fathered Josiah.|Follows pinned Amos rather than harmonizing to Amon.
1:11|Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.|Keeps the deportation hinge and the source’s brothers.
1:12|After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel; Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.|Retains the repeated historical hinge before the next generation group.
1:13|Zerubbabel fathered Abiud; Abiud fathered Eliakim; Eliakim fathered Azor.|Preserves all three otherwise unexplained links.
1:14|Azor fathered Zadok; Zadok fathered Achim; Achim fathered Eliud.|Maintains the genealogy’s deliberately repeated cadence.
1:15|Eliud fathered Eleazar; Eleazar fathered Matthan; Matthan fathered Jacob.|Retains the exact final three links before Joseph.
1:16|Jacob fathered Joseph, Mary’s husband. From her was born Jesus, who is called the Messiah.|Makes the feminine from-whom referent explicit and preserves the switch to passive birth.

1:17|So there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the deportation to Babylon, and fourteen from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah.|Retains all three fourteens and historical boundaries without repairing the literary count.

1:18|This is how the birth of Jesus the Messiah came about. His mother Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together she was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit.|Preserves binding betrothal, prior-to-union timing, and divine agency.

1:19|Her husband Joseph was righteous and did not want to expose her to public disgrace, so he decided to divorce her quietly.|Keeps righteousness alongside restraint and renders the legal separation clearly.

1:20|While he was considering this, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. “Joseph, son of David,” he said, “do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. The child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.|Keeps Davidic address, dream, and conception’s source.
1:21|She will bear a son, and you must name him Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.”|Preserves Joseph’s naming responsibility and salvation from sins, with name-wordplay noted.
1:22|All this happened to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet:|Retains the first fulfillment formula and both divine and prophetic agency.

1:23|“Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son,\nand they will name him Emmanuel,”\nwhich means “God with us.”|Follows Matthew’s Greek virgin and plural they-will-name, preserving the text’s own translation.
1:24|When Joseph woke, he did what the angel of the Lord had commanded and took his wife home.|Keeps waking, obedience, and receiving Mary as linked actions.

1:25|But he did not have sexual relations with her until she bore a son. He named him Jesus.|Makes knew explicit while leaving what follows until unstated and retaining the pinned absence of firstborn.
2:1|After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, during King Herod’s reign, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem.|Retains magi without adding kings, number, or names.

2:2|“Where is the one born king of the Jews?” they asked. “We saw his star at its rising and have come to bow before him.”|Keeps born king and the rising/east ambiguity in a note; bowing does not predetermine the visitors’ theology.
2:3|When King Herod heard this, he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him.|Preserves the city’s shared disturbance without inventing its motive.
2:4|He gathered all the people’s chief priests and scribes and asked them where the Messiah was to be born.|Keeps both named groups and the expected birth-location question.
2:5|“In Bethlehem of Judea,” they told him, “for this is what was written through the prophet:|Retains the quoted scriptural basis and regional identification.

2:6|‘And you, Bethlehem in Judah’s land,
are by no means least among Judah’s rulers,
for from you will come a ruler
who will shepherd my people Israel.’”|Follows Matthew’s quotation rather than harmonizing its wording to Micah’s Hebrew.
2:7|Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and determined from them exactly when the star had appeared.|Preserves secrecy and precise chronological inquiry.

2:8|He sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search carefully for the child. When you find him, report back to me, so I too can go and bow before him.”|Keeps Herod’s professed purpose in his own speech without endorsing it.

2:9|After hearing the king, they went on their way. The star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them until it stopped over the place where the child was.|Retains the star’s narrative movement without substituting an astronomical explanation.
2:10|When they saw the star, they were overwhelmed with joy.|Carries the piled-up Greek intensification into natural English.

2:11|They entered the house and saw the child with Mary his mother. They fell down and bowed before him. Then they opened their treasure chests and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.|Preserves house, mother, bodily homage, and all three gifts.
2:12|Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home by another route.|Retains dream warning and changed route without supplying the warning’s speaker.

2:13|After they left, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. “Get up,” he said. “Take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, because Herod is about to search for the child to kill him.”|Keeps flight, destination, waiting condition, and explicit threatened killing.
2:14|Joseph got up, took the child and his mother during the night, and left for Egypt.|Preserves the urgent nighttime response and repeated child/mother wording.

2:15|He stayed there until Herod’s death. This fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”|Retains fulfillment and the quotation without rewriting Hosea’s earlier context.

2:16|When Herod realized the magi had outwitted him, he became furious. He sent men to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and the surrounding district who were two years old or younger, according to the time he had learned from the magi.|Preserves deliberate killing, male children, age boundary, location, and the timing link.
2:17|Then what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:|Keeps named prophetic attribution.

2:18|“A voice was heard in Ramah,
weeping and great mourning—
Rachel weeping for her children,
refusing to be comforted,
because they are no more.”|Preserves maternal grief and refusal of comfort without adding closure.
2:19|After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt.|Keeps both death transition and dream location.

2:20|“Get up,” he said. “Take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, because those who sought the child’s life are dead.”|Retains the source’s plural those despite the immediate singular Herod reference.
2:21|Joseph got up, took the child and his mother, and entered the land of Israel.|Preserves the obedient repetition of the command.

2:22|But when he heard that Archelaus ruled Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee.|Keeps named succession, fear, and the second relocation warning.

2:23|He settled in a town called Nazareth, fulfilling what was spoken through the prophets: “He will be called a Nazarene.”|Preserves plural prophets and the unassigned quotation rather than inventing a single source.
3:1|In those days John the Baptist appeared in the Judean wilderness, proclaiming,|Keeps wilderness, title, and the announcement’s narrative arrival.
3:2|“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near!”|Retains repentance and the kingdom’s nearness as a recurring formula.

3:3|This is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet:
“A voice cries out in the wilderness:
‘Prepare the Lord’s way;
make his paths straight.’”|Keeps the quotation’s voice, wilderness, and road-preparation imagery.
3:4|John wore clothing made of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.|Retains all concrete clothing and food details without modern substitutes.
3:5|People from Jerusalem, all Judea, and the whole Jordan region went out to him.|Makes the geographical collective subjects natural while retaining their broad scope.
3:6|They confessed their sins and were baptized by him in the Jordan River.|Keeps confession and baptism together without asserting a technical order beyond narrative flow.

3:7|When he saw many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee the coming wrath?|Preserves the named groups, biting insult, and question about warning.
3:8|Produce fruit worthy of repentance.|Retains the fruit image and repentance connection.

3:9|Do not think you can say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ I tell you, God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.|Keeps ancestral claim and stones/children reversal without adding a doctrine of replacement.
3:10|The ax is already lying at the trees’ root. Every tree that fails to produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.|Preserves already, root, and the repeated fruit judgment.

3:11|I baptize you in water for repentance. But the one coming after me is stronger than I am; I am not worthy even to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.|Keeps water/Spirit/fire and carrying sandals rather than harmonizing to untying them.

3:12|His winnowing fork is in his hand. He will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the storehouse, but burn the chaff with fire that cannot be put out.”|Retains each agricultural implement/action and the fire’s unquenchability.
3:13|Then Jesus came from Galilee to John at the Jordan to be baptized by him.|Keeps Jesus’ stated purpose and locations.
3:14|John tried to stop him. “I need to be baptized by you,” he said, “and you come to me?”|Retains John’s attempted resistance and surprised question.

3:15|Jesus answered, “Allow it for now. This is how it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then John allowed him.|Preserves now, us, righteousness, and the repeated allowing without overexplaining the theology.

3:16|After Jesus was baptized, he immediately came up from the water. The heavens opened, and he saw God’s Spirit descending like a dove and coming upon him.|Keeps the visual subject he and the dove comparison rather than declaring a literal bird.
3:17|A voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son; in him I delight.”|Preserves third-person public declaration and divine delight.
4:1|Then the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness to be tested by the devil.|Keeps the Spirit’s leading and the devil’s testing as distinct roles.
4:2|He fasted for forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.|Retains both forty periods and the bodily hunger.
4:3|The tempter approached him and said, “If you are God’s Son, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”|Preserves conditional challenge and plural stones/loaves.

4:4|Jesus answered, “It is written, ‘A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from God’s mouth.’”|Keeps the scriptural answer and mouth image with inclusive human referent.
4:5|Then the devil took him into the holy city and placed him on the temple’s high edge.|Retains holy city and the uncertain architectural edge without inventing a precise height.

4:6|“If you are God’s Son,” he said, “throw yourself down. For it is written:
‘He will command his angels concerning you,’
and,
‘They will lift you on their hands,
so your foot will not strike a stone.’”|Preserves the devil’s scriptural citation and both quoted clauses.
4:7|Jesus told him, “It is also written, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”|Retains the balancing scriptural reply and test verb.
4:8|Again the devil took him, this time to a very high mountain, and showed him all the world’s kingdoms and their glory.|Keeps the comprehensive kingdoms/glory offer and mountain setting.
4:9|“I will give you all of this,” he said, “if you fall down and worship me.”|Retains the explicit exchange condition and bodily submission.
4:10|Jesus said, “Go away, Satan! For it is written, ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.’”|Keeps Satan’s name, both worship/service verbs, and exclusive alone.
4:11|Then the devil left him, and angels came and attended to him.|Retains departure followed by angelic service.
4:12|When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew to Galilee.|Preserves handed-over wording that recurs in the Gospel, with arrest context in a note.
4:13|He left Nazareth and settled in Capernaum beside the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali.|Keeps settlement, shoreline, and both tribal names.
4:14|This fulfilled what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet:|Retains the named fulfillment introduction.

4:15|“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali,\nthe road by the sea, beyond the Jordan,\nGalilee of the nations—|Keeps every geographical element and nations rather than silently interpreting the population.
4:16|the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light;\nfor those sitting in the land and shadow of death,\nlight has dawned.”|Preserves sitting repeated and light/darkness/death imagery.
4:17|From then on Jesus began to proclaim, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near!”|Repeats John’s proclamation exactly to preserve narrative continuity.

4:18|Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.|Retains both names, kinship, and fishing action.
4:19|“Come after me,” he said, “and I will make you fishers of people.”|Preserves the fishing metaphor and inclusive object without replacing it with recruitment explanation.
4:20|At once they left their nets and followed him.|Keeps immediate response and concrete abandoned equipment.

4:21|Going farther, he saw two more brothers, James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in the boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets. He called them,|Retains the full family scene and net-mending work.
4:22|and at once they left the boat and their father and followed him.|Keeps both things left and the repeated immediate following.

4:23|He traveled throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and illness among the people.|Retains teaching/proclamation/healing as three distinct activities.

4:24|Word about him spread throughout Syria. People brought him everyone suffering from various diseases and severe pain, those afflicted by demons, those with seizures, and those who were paralyzed. He healed them.|Preserves the distinct afflictions without conflating seizures with demonic possession.
4:25|Large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.|Keeps all five places and the broad following.
5:1|When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to him,|Keeps setting, teaching posture, and distinct disciples within the crowd scene.
5:2|and he began to teach them:|Renders opened-his-mouth as the beginning of formal speech.
5:3|“Blessed are the poor in spirit,\nfor the kingdom of heaven is theirs.|Retains the qualification in spirit and present possession rather than paraphrasing the blessing.
5:4|Blessed are those who mourn,\nfor they will be comforted.|Keeps mourning broad and the passive future comfort.
5:5|Blessed are the gentle,\nfor they will inherit the earth.|Renders praus as gentle with meekness noted, retaining inheritance and earth/land range.
5:6|Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,\nfor they will be filled.|Preserves both bodily desires and righteousness as a recurring term.
5:7|Blessed are the merciful,\nfor they will receive mercy.|Keeps the mercy reciprocity with clear passive sense.
5:8|Blessed are the pure in heart,\nfor they will see God.|Retains heart and seeing without adding an explanation of purity.
5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers,\nfor they will be called God’s children.|Uses children for the inclusive human group while retaining the divine-family image.
5:10|Blessed are those persecuted for righteousness,\nfor the kingdom of heaven is theirs.|Matches the opening kingdom promise and retains persecution’s stated cause.
5:11|You are blessed when people insult you, persecute you, and falsely say every kind of evil against you because of me.|Keeps the shift to direct address, falsity, and because-of-me qualification.
5:12|Rejoice and celebrate, because your reward in heaven is great. That is how they persecuted the prophets before you.|Retains both joy commands and the prophetic continuity.

5:13|You are the salt of the earth. But if salt loses its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot.|Keeps the riddle and concrete fate without replacing salt with its supposed function.
5:14|You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.|Retains both light and elevated-city images.
5:15|No one lights a lamp and puts it under a grain basket. They put it on a lampstand, where it shines for everyone in the house.|Preserves the household objects and universal household benefit.
5:16|In the same way, let your light shine before people, so they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.|Keeps the purpose directed to the Father rather than personal recognition.
5:17|Do not think I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I came to fulfill them, not to abolish them.|Retains both scriptural divisions and repeated abolish/fulfill contrast.

5:18|Truly I tell you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one smallest letter or pen stroke will pass from the Law until everything happens.|Preserves both until clauses and the exactness image without specifying what everything must mean.

5:19|So whoever sets aside even one of these least commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever practices and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.|Retains least/great and doing/teaching parallels.

5:20|For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will certainly not enter the kingdom of heaven.|Keeps the strong negative and righteousness comparison without caricaturing the named groups.
5:21|You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘Do not murder,’ and, ‘Whoever murders will answer to the court.’|Preserves address to earlier people and both quoted clauses.

5:22|But I tell you: anyone angry with a brother or sister will answer to the court. Whoever calls a brother or sister ‘Raca’ will answer to the council, and whoever says ‘Fool!’ will answer to fiery Gehenna.|Follows the pinned absence of without-cause, retains Raca/Gehenna with vocabulary support, and keeps the escalating judgments.

5:23|So if you are bringing your gift to the altar and remember there that a brother or sister has something against you,|Keeps the grievance as held by the other person and leaves the condition open.
5:24|leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled with that person; then come and offer your gift.|Preserves the order of reconciliation before offering.

5:25|Come to terms with your accuser quickly while you are on the way together. Otherwise your accuser may hand you to the judge, the judge to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.|Keeps the legal progression and urgency of action on the way.
5:26|Truly I tell you: you will not get out until you have paid the last quadrans.|Retains the smallest-debt image and ancient coin with vocabulary help.
5:27|You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’|Retains the quotation without a later textual expansion.

5:28|But I tell you: anyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.|Keeps purposeful looking, specific male/woman relationship, and inner adultery; does not turn all noticing into the claim.

5:29|If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away. It is better to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into Gehenna.|Preserves disturbing hyperbole, right eye, and part/whole contrast, with literary form noted.

5:30|And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away. It is better to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to go into Gehenna.|Keeps the repeated hand version and source’s slightly different final verb.
5:31|It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’|Preserves the gendered legal setting and written certificate.

5:32|But I tell you: anyone who divorces his wife, except on grounds of sexual immorality, causes her to be involved in adultery, and anyone who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.|Retains exception, causative responsibility, and passive involvement, with porneia and syntax explained briefly rather than used as pastoral advice.
5:33|Again, you have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘Do not swear falsely, but fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’|Keeps both prohibitory and positive oath obligations.
5:34|But I tell you not to swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne,|Retains comprehensive prohibition and first supporting image.
5:35|nor by earth, because it is his footstool, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.|Preserves both further referents and reasons.
5:36|Do not swear by your own head either, because you cannot make a single hair white or black.|Keeps the bodily example and exact single-hair limit.
5:37|Let your words be ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no.’ Anything beyond this comes from evil.|Preserves repeated yes/no and leaves evil/evil-one ambiguity noted.
5:38|You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’|Retains the familiar legal formula rather than changing it for novelty.

5:39|But I tell you not to resist the wrongdoer. If someone strikes your right cheek, turn the other to him too.|Keeps the force of nonresistance and specific right cheek without inserting an interpretive limit.
5:40|If someone wants to sue you for your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.|Preserves legal setting and distinct inner/outer garments.
5:41|If someone forces you to go one mile, go two with him.|Keeps coercion and exact one/two contrast.
5:42|Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away someone who wants to borrow from you.|Retains separate giving and lending commands.
5:43|You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’|Keeps the cited saying without falsely assigning the entire phrase to Torah in a note.
5:44|But I tell you: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,|Follows the shorter pinned text and keeps both enemy-love and prayer.

5:45|so you may be children of your Father in heaven. He makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.|Preserves divine-family purpose and both weather gifts across moral contrasts.
5:46|If you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even tax collectors do the same?|Keeps the rhetorical question and named comparison group.

5:47|And if you greet only your own brothers and sisters, what more are you doing? Do not even Gentiles do the same?|Preserves greeting, exclusive circle, and nations without importing a new insult. Renders ethnikoí as Gentiles, identifying non-Jewish people rather than political nations.
5:48|So be complete, as your heavenly Father is complete.|Keeps the telos/wholeness force in context, with perfect as a lexical alternative noted.

6:1|Be careful not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them. Otherwise you have no reward from your Father in heaven.|Follows pinned righteousness and preserves the motive qualification linking the examples.

6:2|So when you give to the poor, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets to win people’s praise. Truly I tell you: they have received their reward in full.|Keeps almsgiving concrete, the trumpet image, and full-payment refrain.
6:3|But when you give to the poor, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,|Preserves the impossible secrecy image rather than converting it to advice about bookkeeping.
6:4|so your giving may be in secret. Your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.|Keeps the secret/seeing contrast and no added openly.

6:5|When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. They love to stand praying in synagogues and on street corners so people will see them. Truly I tell you: they have received their reward in full.|Retains visibility motive and repeats the reward refrain exactly.

6:6|But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is in secret. Your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.|Preserves private-room sequence and repeated secret language.

6:7|When you pray, do not babble like Gentiles. They think they will be heard because of their many words.|Keeps the critique of speech and presumed efficacy without treating all repeated prayer as condemned. Renders ethnikoí as Gentiles, identifying non-Jewish people rather than political nations.
6:8|Do not be like them. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.|Retains divine knowledge before asking without deleting the call to prayer.
6:9|Pray like this:\n‘Our Father in heaven,\nmay your name be held holy.|Keeps plural our and passive sanctification as a petition.
6:10|May your kingdom come.\nMay your will be done\non earth as in heaven.|Preserves three parallel petitions and earthly realization.
6:11|Give us today the bread we need.|Chooses needed bread for epiousios, with daily/coming-day alternatives noted.
6:12|Forgive us our debts,\nas we too have forgiven our debtors.|Retains debts metaphor and pinned past have-forgiven.
6:13|Do not bring us into testing,\nbut rescue us from evil.’|Keeps the difficult divine-agency petition, evil/evil-one ambiguity, and absence of later doxology.
6:14|For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.|Preserves the conditional reciprocity and transition from debts to offenses.
6:15|But if you do not forgive people, your Father will not forgive your offenses.|Keeps the negative counterpart without adding an unstated object to the first clause.

6:16|When you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites. They disfigure their faces so people will notice they are fasting. Truly I tell you: they have received their reward in full.|Preserves appearance motive and the third exact reward refrain.
6:17|But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,|Keeps the ordinary grooming actions rather than a modern equivalent.
6:18|so your fasting is seen by your Father who is in secret, not by people. Your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.|Retains the visibility contrast and repeated private reward wording.
6:19|Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and decay destroy and thieves break in and steal.|Keeps moth, consuming decay, and burglary images.
6:20|Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor decay destroys and thieves do not break in or steal.|Mirrors the preceding sentence to retain its contrast and repetition.
6:21|For where your treasure is, there your heart will be too.|Retains singular your and the familiar heart/treasure relation.
6:22|The eye is the body’s lamp. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.|Keeps eye/lamp and whole-body light; single/generous nuances noted.

6:23|But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be dark. If the light within you is darkness, how great that darkness is!|Preserves the paradox and exclamation without reducing it to eyesight advice.

6:24|No one can serve two masters. You will hate one and love the other, or be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.|Keeps slavery-service, opposed allegiances, and mammon as wealth with vocabulary support.

6:25|That is why I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. Is life not more than food, and the body more than clothing?|Follows the pinned shorter first list and keeps the life/body comparison.

6:26|Look at the birds of heaven. They neither sow nor reap nor gather into storehouses, yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they are?|Preserves all three agricultural absences and rhetorical comparison.
6:27|Which of you can add a single cubit to your lifespan by worrying?|Retains the deliberately mixed measurement image and notes stature/lifespan ambiguity.
6:28|And why worry about clothing? Consider how the field’s lilies grow. They neither labor nor spin,|Keeps the observation invitation and both absent forms of work.
6:29|yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of them.|Retains specific royal comparison and single flower.

6:30|If God clothes the field’s grass this way, though it is here today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, will he not clothe you much more, you of little faith?|Preserves ephemeral fuel, divine provision, and direct faith rebuke.
6:31|So do not worry, asking, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’|Retains all three practical questions in their repeated form.
6:32|The nations seek all these things, and your heavenly Father knows you need them all.|Keeps nations, all twice, and the Father’s knowledge.
6:33|Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.|Follows pinned absence of of-God after kingdom and preserves righteousness and priority.
6:34|So do not worry about tomorrow. Tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.|Retains personified tomorrow and the limited daily horizon.
7:1|Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.|Keeps the uncompromising command and passive consequence.
7:2|For the judgment you give will be given to you, and the measure you use will be used for you.|Preserves the two reciprocal images and passive agency.
7:3|Why do you notice the speck in your brother’s or sister’s eye but fail to consider the beam in your own?|Retains the absurd scale contrast and inclusive fellow-member referent.
7:4|How can you say, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ when there is a beam in your own eye?|Keeps quoted offer and self-contradictory situation.
7:5|Hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye. Then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s or sister’s eye.|Preserves first/then order and the eventual ability to help.

7:6|Do not give what is holy to dogs or throw your pearls before pigs. They may trample them underfoot, then turn and tear you apart.|Retains animals, precious objects, and violent reversal without assigning modern groups to them.
7:7|Ask, and it will be given to you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and the door will be opened to you.|Preserves the three parallel commands and promises.
7:8|For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened.|Retains the complete repetition in indicative form.
7:9|Who among you would give his son a stone when he asks for bread?|Keeps father/son and the food/stone contrast.
7:10|Or give him a snake when he asks for a fish?|Preserves the parallel question and specific animals.

7:11|If you, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!|Retains the troubling evil assessment and greater divine generosity without importing Luke’s Spirit wording.
7:12|So in everything, do for others what you want them to do for you. This is the Law and the Prophets.|Keeps comprehensive scope, active obligation, and scriptural summary.
7:13|Enter through the narrow gate. The gate is wide and the road spacious that leads to destruction, and many enter through it.|Preserves both gate and road and the many travelers.
7:14|But the gate is narrow and the road constricted that leads to life, and few find it.|Keeps the constrained road and few without turning the image into statistics.
7:15|Watch out for false prophets. They come to you dressed as sheep, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.|Retains disguise, inward reality, and predatory force.
7:16|You will recognize them by their fruit. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?|Keeps the fruit criterion and both botanical questions.
7:17|In the same way, every good tree produces good fruit, while a rotten tree produces bad fruit.|Retains tree/fruit relation and rotten rather than merely different.
7:18|A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree produce good fruit.|Preserves the repeated impossibility and reverse parallel.
7:19|Every tree that fails to produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.|Matches the recurring judgment wording from chapter three.
7:20|So you will recognize them by their fruit.|Retains the closing repetition of the criterion.
7:21|Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does my heavenly Father’s will.|Preserves repeated Lord and the contrast between speech and doing.

7:22|Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, drive out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’|Keeps all three claims and three in-your-name repetitions.
7:23|Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness!’|Preserves never, personal rejection, and lawlessness without softening it.
7:24|So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.|Keeps hearing/doing and the wise builder with concrete foundation.

7:25|The rain came down, the rivers rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house. But it did not fall, because its foundation was on rock.|Preserves all three pressures and the stated reason for survival.
7:26|Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on sand.|Mirrors the prior builder while retaining the decisive failure to act.
7:27|The rain came down, the rivers rose, and the winds blew and struck that house. It fell, and its fall was great.”|Retains repeated storm sequence and emphatic collapse.
7:28|When Jesus finished saying these things, the crowds were astonished at his teaching,|Keeps the discourse-ending formula and crowd response.
7:29|because he taught them as someone with authority, unlike their scribes.|Retains the narrator’s explanation and specific comparison without broad claims about Judaism.
8:1|When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him.|Names the returning subject and preserves the movement from teaching to encounter.
8:2|A man with a skin disease came up, bowed before him, and said, “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”|Keeps willingness distinct from ability and avoids a modern diagnosis for lepros.

8:3|Jesus reached out and touched him. “I am willing,” he said. “Be clean.” At once the man’s skin disease was cleansed.|Retains touch, verbal echo, and immediate cleansing rather than only medical recovery.

8:4|Then Jesus told him, “See that you tell no one. Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”|Preserves the prohibition and ritual testimony without specifying its disputed audience.
8:5|As Jesus entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, pleading,|Keeps the military title and lets the plea continue across the label.
8:6|“Lord, my servant is lying at home, paralyzed and suffering terribly.”|Renders pais as servant in context while preserving paralysis and severe suffering.
8:7|Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.”|Retains the emphatic personal offer; the possible question belongs in a note.
8:8|The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed.|Preserves roof imagery and confidence in a spoken command.

8:9|I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”|Distinguishes doulos from pais and preserves each command and response.

8:10|When Jesus heard this, he was amazed. He told those following him, “Truly I tell you, I have found no one in Israel with faith like this.|Keeps the source’s comparative claim without adding universal ethnic judgment.

8:11|And I tell you, many will come from east and west and take their places at the feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.|Makes reclining intelligible as a feast while retaining named ancestors and directions.
8:12|But the heirs of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and grinding of teeth.”|Renders sons idiomatically as heirs but retains exclusion and judgment imagery.
8:13|Then Jesus told the centurion, “Go. Let it happen for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very hour.|Preserves the direct address and precise correspondence in time.
8:14|Jesus went into Peter’s house and saw Peter’s mother-in-law lying sick with a fever.|Makes the relationship explicit without adding a household history.
8:15|He touched her hand, and the fever left her. She got up and began serving him.|Retains female agency and the singular recipient of service.

8:16|That evening, people brought him many who were possessed by demons. He drove out the spirits with a word and healed everyone who was ill.|Distinguishes spirits from illness and retains comprehensive healing.

8:17|This fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:\n“He took our weaknesses\nand carried our diseases.”|Keeps Matthew’s bodily wording and shapes the quotation as poetry within its verse.
8:18|When Jesus saw the large crowds around him, he gave orders to cross to the other side.|Preserves the source’s plural crowds and unspecified destination shore.
8:19|A scribe came up and said, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.”|Retains the trained role and the unqualified offer.

8:20|Jesus answered him, “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”|Keeps the title and complete animal contrast rather than explaining away the image.
8:21|Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”|Preserves first and the actual request without inventing circumstances of death.
8:22|But Jesus told him, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”|Retains the disturbing double use of dead without resolving its metaphor in the text.
8:23|Jesus got into a boat, and his disciples followed him.|Keeps following visible as both action and narrative theme.
8:24|Suddenly a violent disturbance swept over the sea, and waves were covering the boat. But Jesus was asleep.|Renders seismos strongly without deciding that an earthquake caused the waves.
8:25|They went to him and woke him. “Lord, save us!” they said. “We’re going to die!”|Keeps the urgent salvation plea and immediate danger in natural speech.

8:26|He said to them, “Why are you so afraid, you of little faith?” Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm came over it.|Retains little faith, rebuke, and the great disturbance/great calm contrast.
8:27|The men were amazed. “What kind of man is this,” they said, “that even the winds and the sea obey him?”|Preserves their unresolved question and the scope of obedience.

8:28|When he reached the other side, in the region of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men came out from the tombs to meet him. They were so violent that no one could pass along that road.|Retains two men and the pinned place name without harmonizing other accounts.
8:29|They shouted, “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the appointed time?”|Preserves title, antagonistic idiom, and premature judgment question.
8:30|A large herd of pigs was feeding some distance away.|Keeps distance and herd size without locating an unmentioned owner.
8:31|The demons begged him, “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”|Retains the conditional request and its actual destination.

8:32|“Go,” he told them. They came out and went into the pigs. Then the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the water.|Preserves the lethal outcome and every stage without softening the loss.

8:33|The herders ran away. They went into the town and reported everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.|Makes the compressed report intelligible without supplying unreported reactions.
8:34|The whole town came out to meet Jesus. When they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.|Keeps the collective response and unexpected request to depart.
9:1|Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own town.|Retains own town without inserting its inferred name.

9:2|Some people brought him a paralyzed man lying on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, he told the man, “Take courage, child. Your sins are forgiven.”|Keeps their plural faith and the affectionate singular address.
9:3|Some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”|Preserves the inward accusation without endorsing it as narrator.
9:4|Jesus knew what they were thinking. “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” he asked.|Keeps the heart image and explicit moral challenge.
9:5|“Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?|Retains the comparison between sayings, not a claim that either act is easy.

9:6|But so that you may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralyzed man, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”|Preserves the interrupted sentence and changed addressee.
9:7|The man got up and went home.|Keeps the concise enacted response without embellishment.
9:8|When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.|Follows fear and plural humans rather than harmonizing to amazement or Jesus alone.

9:9|As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. “Follow me,” he told him. Matthew got up and followed him.|Keeps the call-response pattern and names the actor for clarity.

9:10|While Jesus was reclining at a meal in the house, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with him and his disciples.|Retains reclining and avoids assigning ownership to the unspecified house.
9:11|The Pharisees saw this and asked his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”|Keeps the question directed to disciples and the repeated social categories.
9:12|Jesus heard them and said, “Healthy people don’t need a doctor; sick people do.|Preserves the compact analogy in ordinary spoken English.
9:13|Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I came to call sinners, not the righteous.”|Keeps the scriptural contrast and excludes an unprinted addition about repentance.
9:14|Then John’s disciples came to him. “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often,” they asked, “but your disciples don’t fast?”|Preserves often and both groups without generalizing their practice.

9:15|Jesus said to them, “Can wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them. Then they will fast.|Renders sons of the bridal chamber accessibly and preserves the passive removal.
9:16|No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. The patch pulls away from the garment, making the tear worse.|Makes the material action clear without allegorical explanation.

9:17|Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins burst, the wine spills, and the skins are ruined. They put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”|Preserves both kinds of loss and the final preservation of both.

9:18|While he was telling them these things, a ruler came and bowed before him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”|Retains has just died and avoids importing a different chronology or office.
9:19|Jesus got up and followed him, along with his disciples.|Preserves Jesus now following the petitioner and the accompanying disciples.
9:20|Just then, a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment.|Retains duration, approach, and the particular part touched.
9:21|She had been saying to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be healed.”|Uses healed for contextual saved while retaining the conditional inner speech.

9:22|Jesus turned, saw her, and said, “Take courage, daughter. Your faith has made you well.” From that moment the woman was healed.|Keeps daughter and the repeated saving/healing language in its bodily setting.
9:23|When Jesus reached the ruler’s house, he saw the flute players and the noisy crowd.|Retains the audible mourning scene without adding hired status.
9:24|“Go away,” he said. “The girl isn’t dead; she is sleeping.” But they laughed at him.|Preserves Jesus’ assertion and ridicule without explaining sleep in the dialogue.
9:25|After the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her hand, and the girl got up.|Keeps the passive removal and simple rising without added spectacle.
9:26|News of this spread through that entire region.|Keeps the local scope of the report.
9:27|As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, calling out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”|Preserves two, the royal title, and the plea for mercy.
9:28|When he entered the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus asked them, “Do you believe I can do this?” “Yes, Lord,” they answered.|Keeps the question about ability and direct collective answer.
9:29|Then he touched their eyes and said, “Let it happen for you according to your faith.”|Retains physical contact and according to without adding a measurable degree.
9:30|Their eyes were opened. Jesus warned them sternly, “See that no one learns about this.”|Preserves the strong warning rather than a casual request.
9:31|But they went out and spread news of him throughout that region.|Keeps the contrast between instruction and actual conduct.
9:32|As they were leaving, people brought him a demon-possessed man who could not speak.|Renders kophos by the speech outcome rather than assuming deafness.
9:33|Once the demon was driven out, the man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”|Preserves sequence and the crowd’s sweeping reported claim.
9:34|But the Pharisees said, “He drives out demons by the ruler of demons.”|Retains the counterclaim without presenting it as narrator’s explanation.

9:35|Jesus traveled through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity.|Preserves the three coordinated activities and repeated every.
9:36|When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them. They were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.|Retains both conditions and the biblical shepherd image.
9:37|Then he told his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.|Keeps the large harvest/small workforce contrast.
9:38|So ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers out into his harvest.”|Preserves ownership repeated in the appeal and destination.

10:1|Jesus called his twelve disciples to him and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to drive them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity.|Keeps twelve and the authority linking this mission with Jesus’ work.
10:2|These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee and his brother John;|Preserves first and the paired family relationships.
10:3|Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus;|Retains all names and Matthew’s occupation without harmonizing alternate lists.
10:4|Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot, who also handed Jesus over.|Renders Kanana ios as a designation of zeal and links betrayal to handed over.
10:5|Jesus sent these twelve out with these instructions: “Do not go among the Gentiles or enter a Samaritan town.|Preserves the restricted destination of this particular commission.
10:6|Go instead to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.|Keeps the house and sheep images without replacing them with an abstract audience.
10:7|As you go, proclaim, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’|Matches the established proclamation formula and sense of nearness.

10:8|Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those with skin diseases, drive out demons. You received without paying; give without charging.|Preserves all four imperatives and the free receiving/giving balance.
10:9|Do not get gold, silver, or copper for your belts,|Keeps all three metals and the ancient carrying image.
10:10|or a travel bag, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff. A worker deserves food.|Retains Matthew’s actual equipment restrictions without harmonizing other Gospels.
10:11|Whatever town or village you enter, find out who there is worthy, and stay with that person until you leave.|Preserves discernment of a host and stable lodging.
10:12|As you enter the house, greet it.|Keeps the household addressed through the house image.
10:13|If the house is worthy, let your peace rest on it. If it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.|Preserves the conditional movement of peace in both directions.
10:14|If anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, shake the dust from your feet as you leave that house or town.|Keeps both refusals and the embodied departure sign.
10:15|Truly I tell you, on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town.|Preserves comparative judgment and both named cities.
10:16|“Look, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. So be shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves.|Retains all four animals and pairs practical discernment with innocence.
10:17|Watch out for people. They will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues.|Keeps concrete institutional persecution without generalizing it to all Jews.
10:18|You will be brought before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.|Preserves purpose, audiences, and cause.
10:19|When they hand you over, do not worry about how to speak or what to say. What you should say will be given to you at that time.|Keeps both anxieties and the passive gift at the needed moment.
10:20|For it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.|Preserves the personal Father relationship and Spirit’s agency.
10:21|Brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his child. Children will turn against their parents and have them put to death.|Keeps the family roles and actual lethal consequences.
10:22|Everyone will hate you because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.|Retains the sweeping warning and future promise without resolving end’s referent.

10:23|When they persecute you in one town, flee to another. Truly I tell you, you will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.|Preserves the difficult temporal claim without inserting a later interpretive timetable.
10:24|“A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master.|Keeps both unequal relationships and the source’s slave term.

10:25|It is enough for the disciple to become like the teacher, and the slave like the master. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign his household!|Makes the elliptical final comparison readable while retaining the household image and name.
10:26|So do not fear them. Nothing covered up will stay unrevealed, and nothing hidden will remain unknown.|Preserves the paired disclosure assurances and their causal link.
10:27|What I tell you in the dark, speak in the light. What you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim from the rooftops.|Retains dark/light and ear/rooftop contrasts.

10:28|Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear instead the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.|Keeps soul/body distinction and destroy without importing a theory of punishment.
10:29|Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father.|Retains coin and the source’s open apart-from phrase rather than specifying causation.
10:30|Even the hairs on your head have all been counted.|Preserves the surprising totality of the image.
10:31|So do not be afraid. You are worth more than many sparrows.|Keeps the many contrast and reassurance grounded in the preceding image.
10:32|“Everyone who acknowledges me before others, I too will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.|Preserves reciprocal public acknowledgment.
10:33|But whoever denies me before others, I too will deny before my Father in heaven.|Keeps the exact opposing structure and consequence.
10:34|“Do not think I came to bring peace to the earth. I came to bring a sword, not peace.|Retains the sharp image before its explanation in family division.
10:35|For I came to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.|Preserves all three specifically gendered relationships.
10:36|A person’s enemies will be members of that person’s own household.|Keeps the household focus of the preceding sword image.

10:37|Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.|Preserves comparative love and both generations without substituting hatred.
10:38|Whoever does not take up their cross and follow me is not worthy of me.|Retains the execution image and repeated worthiness language.
10:39|Whoever finds their life will lose it, and whoever loses their life because of me will find it.|Keeps the paradox and explicit because-of-me qualification.
10:40|“Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.|Preserves the linked chain of welcome and sending.

10:41|Whoever welcomes a prophet because that person is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. Whoever welcomes a righteous person because that person is righteous will receive a righteous person’s reward.|Unfolds in the name of without losing the repeated identities and rewards.

10:42|And whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because that person is a disciple—truly I tell you, that giver will certainly not lose the reward.”|Preserves the small gift, little ones, disciple qualification, and emphatic assurance.

11:1|When Jesus finished instructing his twelve disciples, he left that place to teach and proclaim his message in their towns.|Preserves the discourse conclusion and the source’s their without inventing a route.

11:3|to ask Jesus, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect someone else?”|Retains the coming-one expression and the genuine alternative in John’s question.

11:9|Then what did you go out for? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.|Follows the pinned punctuation’s emphatic final identification.

11:12|From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and violent people seize it.|Chooses the passive reading of biazetai with the competing sense reserved for a note.

11:14|And if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.|Preserves the conditional invitation and explicit identification.
11:15|Let anyone with ears listen.|Retains the brief listening refrain without an absent expansion.
11:16|“What can I compare this generation to? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, calling to the others,|Keeps the comparison and public setting.

11:20|Then he began denouncing the towns where most of his mighty works had taken place, because they had not repented.|Preserves the explicit reason for denunciation.

22:13|Then the king told the attendants, ‘Bind his feet and hands and throw him into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and grinding of teeth.’|Distinguishes attendants from slaves and retains the judgment refrain.
22:14|For many are called, but few are chosen.”|Keeps the concise called/chosen contrast without doctrinal expansion.
22:15|Then the Pharisees went and planned how to trap him in what he said.|Preserves the explicitly hostile rhetorical purpose.

22:16|They sent their disciples to him with the Herodians. “Teacher,” they said, “we know you are truthful and teach God’s way truthfully. You are not swayed by anyone, because you do not judge by appearances.|Renders face-looking idiom naturally while preserving their flattery.
22:17|So tell us what you think: Is it permitted to pay tribute to Caesar or not?”|Keeps the legal question and Roman recipient.
22:18|Jesus knew their malice. “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?” he asked.|Preserves narrator’s motive statement and direct rebuke.
22:19|“Show me the coin used for the tribute.” They brought him a denarius.|Keeps the requested object and precise denomination.
22:20|He asked them, “Whose image and inscription are these?”|Retains both identifying features.

22:21|“Caesar’s,” they answered. Then he told them, “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.”|Keeps give-back force and the parallel claims without a political system added.
22:22|When they heard this, they were amazed. They left him and went away.|Preserves the actual response and withdrawal.
22:23|That same day Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, approached him and asked,|Keeps the relevant belief attributed to this group.
22:24|“Teacher, Moses said that if a man dies without children, his brother must marry the widow and raise offspring for his brother.|Preserves the brother’s duty and lineage purpose.
22:25|There were seven brothers among us. The first married and died without offspring, leaving his wife to his brother.|Keeps the hypothetical family’s number and sequence.
22:26|The same happened to the second and third, and on through all seven.|Preserves repetition compressed by the source.
22:27|After all of them, the woman died.|Keeps her death last in sequence.
22:28|So in the resurrection, whose wife will she be of the seven? All of them had married her.”|Preserves the legal puzzle without treating the woman as an object in English.
22:29|Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power.|Keeps the two stated failures.
22:30|In the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage. They are like God’s angels in heaven.|Retains simile rather than saying humans become angels.
22:31|And about the resurrection of the dead, haven’t you read what God said to you:|Preserves the striking to-you address of Scripture.
22:32|‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is God of the living, not of the dead.”|Keeps three repeated titles and the life/death contrast.
22:33|The crowds heard this and were astonished at his teaching.|Retains teaching as the object of astonishment.
22:34|When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together.|Preserves the narrative link between exchanges.
22:35|One of them, an expert in the Law, tested him with a question:|Keeps expertise and testing purpose.
22:36|“Teacher, which commandment is greatest in the Law?”|Renders great contextually as a ranking question.
22:37|He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind.’|Keeps all three faculties and repeated totality without adding strength.
22:38|This is the greatest and first commandment.|Retains both priority terms.
22:39|A second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’|Keeps likeness and self-comparison.
22:40|The whole Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”|Preserves the hanging image and comprehensive scope.
22:41|While the Pharisees were gathered, Jesus asked them,|Keeps the reversal to Jesus as questioner.
22:42|“What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?” “David’s,” they answered.|Preserves Messiah and the lineage question.
22:43|He asked them, “How then does David, speaking in the Spirit, call him Lord? He says,|Keeps Spirit attribution and the posed tension.
22:44|‘The Lord said to my Lord,\n“Sit at my right hand\nuntil I put your enemies beneath your feet.”’|Preserves two Lords, right-hand position, and pinned beneath rather than footstool.
22:45|If David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”|Retains the unanswered interpretive question.
22:46|No one could answer him a word. From that day on, no one dared question him any further.|Keeps both immediate silence and subsequent cessation.
23:1|Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples:|Preserves both audiences before the direct denunciation.
23:2|“The scribes and Pharisees have taken their seat in Moses’s chair.|Keeps the teaching-authority image rather than assigning an unmentioned office.
23:3|So do and observe everything they tell you, but do not act as they act. They speak but do not do.|Preserves the difficult positive instruction alongside the criticism of conduct.
23:4|They tie up heavy loads and put them on people’s shoulders, but will not move them with their own finger.|Retains bodily burden imagery without an absent extra adjective.
23:5|They do everything to be seen by people. They make their phylacteries broad and their garment fringes long.|Keeps specific practices for vocabulary explanation and the stated display motive.
23:6|They love the place of honor at dinners and the front seats in synagogues,|Preserves both settings and sought positions.
23:7|greetings in the marketplaces, and being called ‘Rabbi’ by people.|Keeps title and public recognition.
23:8|But you must not be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers and sisters.|Renders community sibling language inclusively while retaining the one-teacher claim.
23:9|And call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, the heavenly one.|Keeps the force of the saying without embedding an exception.
23:10|Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Messiah.|Distinguishes this title from teacher and retains Messiah.
23:11|The greatest among you will be your servant.|Keeps future formulation and greatness/service reversal.
23:12|Whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted.|Preserves both passive reversals without naming an unstated agent.

23:13|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. You do not enter yourselves, and you do not let those trying to enter go in.|Retains the door image and both failures without adding absent verse14.

23:15|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You travel over sea and land to make one convert, and when you do, you make that person twice as much a child of Gehenna as yourselves.|Keeps travel, one convert, doubled judgment, and family metaphor.

23:16|“Woe to you, blind guides! You say, ‘If anyone swears by the sanctuary, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the sanctuary’s gold, the oath is binding.’|Distinguishes sanctuary from wider temple and preserves the quoted rule.
23:17|Blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the sanctuary that made the gold holy?|Keeps the sharp address and source of holiness.
23:18|You also say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift on it, the oath is binding.’|Preserves the parallel disputed rule.
23:19|Blind people! Which is greater: the gift, or the altar that makes the gift holy?|Follows the pinned shorter address and repeats the sanctifying relation.
23:20|So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it.|Keeps the inclusive oath implication.
23:21|Whoever swears by the sanctuary swears by it and by the one who dwells in it.|Preserves dwelling without replacing the personal referent with an abstraction.
23:22|And whoever swears by heaven swears by God’s throne and by the one seated on it.|Keeps throne and enthroned person distinct in the image.

23:23|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You tithe mint, dill, and cumin, but have neglected the weightier matters of the Law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced these without neglecting the others.|Retains all herbs, three virtues, and the nonexclusive conclusion.
23:24|Blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.|Keeps the deliberately absurd size contrast.

23:25|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of plunder and self-indulgence.|Follows pinned akrasia and preserves the image’s moral contents.
23:26|Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that its outside may become clean too.|Keeps singular addressee, printed dish, and inside-before-outside sequence.

23:27|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside but full of dead people’s bones and every kind of uncleanness within.|Preserves beauty/death contrast and ritual language.
23:28|In the same way, you appear righteous to people on the outside, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.|Keeps the explicit interpretation of the tomb image.
23:29|“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You build the prophets’ tombs and decorate the monuments of the righteous,|Preserves both commemorative activities.
23:30|and say, ‘If we had lived in our ancestors’ days, we would not have shared with them in shedding the prophets’ blood.’|Keeps their counterfactual moral claim and blood imagery.
23:31|So you testify against yourselves that you are descendants of those who murdered the prophets.|Preserves the familial accusation as Jesus’ rhetorical argument.
23:32|You too—fill up the measure of your ancestors!|Retains the biting imperative and measure image without softening to prediction.
23:33|Snakes! Brood of vipers! How will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?|Keeps both insults and the rhetorical judgment question.

23:34|That is why I am sending you prophets, wise people, and scribes. Some you will kill and crucify; others you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town.|Preserves all three sent groups and concrete forms of violence.

23:35|So all the righteous blood shed on earth will come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.|Keeps the difficult patronymic exactly rather than harmonizing to another Zechariah.
23:36|Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.|Preserves this generation as the explicit scope.

23:37|“Jerusalem, Jerusalem! You kill the prophets and stone those sent to you. How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, but you were unwilling!|Retains doubled city name, maternal image, and competing wills.
23:38|Look, your house is left to you deserted.|Follows pinned deserted and leaves house’s referent open.
23:39|For I tell you, from now on you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord’s name.’”|Keeps the temporal qualification and exact earlier acclamation.
